Patient Vignette: "Kofi"

Kofi is a 37-year-old Ghanaian man, a clinical psychologist who specializes in trauma. He arrived at his first session with me precisely on time, his posture rigid, his tailored suit immaculate. He offered a dry, professional smile that did not reach his eyes. He stated his reason for seeking therapy with the same clinical detachment he might use to describe a case study: "I am experiencing a significant stress response following an interpersonal trauma." It was the first of many defenses I would come to recognize.

The trauma occurred eight months ago. Kofi was in Lagos for a week-long conference on vicarious traumatization in humanitarian workers. On the final night, after a banquet, he made the mistake of accepting a ride from a colleague he had known for years, another psychologist named Emeka. They had shared drinks, and Kofi, trusting him, accepted a lift back to his hotel. The next thing he remembers is waking up in a strange room, naked, in excruciating pain. Emeka was gone. The physical evidence of the assault was undeniable.

Kofi did not go to the police. He did not tell his family. He cleaned himself up, caught his flight back to Accra, and went to work the next day. He tells me this part of the story with a flat, even tone. "I compartmentalized," he says, as if explaining a therapeutic technique to a student. "It was a violation. I understood the psychology of it. I knew the recovery model. I simply needed to apply the principles to myself."

But the principles have not applied. For the past eight months, Kofi has been living in a state of silent, high-alert terror. He cannot sleep. He lies awake, listening to the hum of his ceiling fan, replaying the blank space in his memory—the gap between the car ride and waking up. He has not had a full night’s rest since the assault. His PCL-5 score of 61 reflects the profound severity of his symptoms, a number that feels both abstract and devastatingly real.

His work, once his sanctuary, has become a battlefield. He can no longer sit with a patient who describes a sexual assault without his own body reacting. He feels a surge of cold sweat, his heart hammering against his ribs. He has started subtly steering these conversations away from the details, a betrayal of his own clinical ethics that fills him with shame. He finds himself avoiding the male patients on his caseload, unconsciously scheduling them with his intern. He has stopped taking referrals for anyone who has experienced "interpersonal violence." He knows what he is doing is wrong. He knows he is failing his patients. The thought of one of them seeing through his composure, of them sensing the victim in their therapist, is a terror that rivals the assault itself.

He has not dated since the event. The thought of intimacy, of being touched, is nauseating. He has stopped shaking hands with male colleagues. He changed his route to work to avoid a man on the street who vaguely resembles Emeka. He carries a small pocketknife now, a detail he offers with a self-deprecating laugh that sounds more like a gasp.

In our sessions, Kofi sits perfectly still, his hands folded in his lap. He dissects his own symptoms with surgical precision. "The hypervigilance is a classic manifestation of a perceived ongoing threat," he told me last week. "The avoidance is a maladaptive coping strategy to manage the conditioned fear response." He is a brilliant man trapped inside his own clinical textbook, unable to touch the raw, bleeding wound beneath the diagnosis. He is a psychologist who has lost the ability to be a patient.
